Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

I have lost my connection to my community and culture
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette: Aisha, a 35‑year‑old African‑American police officer, was 27 when a night shift ended with a brutal sexual assault that would forever scar her sense of safety. While on patrol in the precinct parking lot, a former colleague—off‑duty and untrustworthy—locked her in an abandoned break room, forcing her into a desperate violation. The night closed with her clutching her jacket, the smell of stale air lingering in her lungs, and her partner’s muffled voice rising and falling in the hallway behind her. The memory never fully faded. The first time it resurfaced, she felt a tightness in her chest that mirrored the exact pressure she had felt when the attacker’s hand brushed her back. Pain radiated to her lower back, the very spot where the assault had happened, and a surge of rage flooded her, making her feel as if the same fury still lived inside her. When she could not remember the man’s face or the precise words he had whispered, an emptiness gnawed at her, leaving her exhausted. Because of this vivid recall of pain and fury, she began to steer clear of any situation that might stir intense emotion— the sirens that wail on a midnight shift, the crowded community outreach events she once enjoyed, even the quiet moments in the break room where she would normally chat with colleagues. She would often replay the night in her mind, wondering how her life might have unfolded had the assault never happened, and in doing so she used that counterfactual thinking as a way to keep the memory alive while avoiding the raw feelings it stirred. The assault also reshaped the way Aisha viewed herself and her community. Each time she could piece together a fragment of the night, she compared herself with the others in her precinct who had never faced such violation, feeling the sting of isolation and believing that “someone else would not have gotten into this situation.” The sense of disconnection grew when she realized she could no longer attend the church services she had attended since childhood, nor the neighborhood festivals that had once been a source of joy. She whispered to herself that she was no longer part of the community, that she had been permanently altered for the worse. These thoughts left her convinced that the world had shifted around her, that she had become a different person, one who could no longer safely step into shared spaces. Because of these harsh self‑appraisals, Aisha began to sidestep confrontation altogether. When a supervisor suggested a new protocol, she would nod and stay silent; if a partner raised a question about a case, she would deflect or leave the conversation abruptly. She feared that any disagreement would expose the scar beneath her exterior, that others might see her as fragile or unsteady. This avoidance of conflict extended into her marriage; she would shut down when her husband tried to discuss their future, retreating into a shell of silence that left their communication strained. The compulsion to avoid friction kept her from addressing the deeper wounds and left her relationship fraying at the edges. The combination of these patterns started to take a toll on Aisha’s career. She began missing shifts because the emotional weight of being on duty felt overwhelming, and the fear of confrontation with colleagues made her reluctant to engage in team briefings. Her partners began to see her as unreliable, and her performance reviews reflected a decline in initiative and teamwork. At home, the silence she maintained about her trauma pushed her husband away, and the once‑joyful gatherings at the community center now seemed like distant memories. The moment that finally pushed Aisha toward therapy was the night she found herself crying at the station after a call that ended with a victim’s sobbing. She could no longer bear the ache of that memory and the constant avoidance it demanded. She feared that if she did not confront what she had lost—the sense of community, the ability to engage without fear, the stability of her marriage—she would continue to deteriorate. Her hope is that through treatment she can untangle the painful memories from her everyday life, reclaim her sense of belonging, and find a way to speak about the event without feeling like it will shatter her again. She seeks to understand how the memory of that night continues to shape her thoughts, and to break the loop that keeps her isolated and disconnected.
